newsitem.title: CANADA: Diamond mine rises from Canada's Arctic tundra.
newsitem.headline: Diamond mine rises from Canada's Arctic tundra.

text.p: In the endless daylight of an Arctic summer, construction crews are working around the clock to transform the Canadian tundra into a high-tech $700 million diamond mine by next year.
Once a barren expanse of tiny lakes and granite boulders, the 450,000-acre property near Lac de Gras in Canada's Northwest Territories now swarms with activity.

Just six years since the discovery of diamonds here, Australian minerals powerhouse Broken Hill Proprietary Co. Ltd., 51 percent owner of the project, is racing to complete construction on Canada's first diamond mine.
On a visit to the remote site this week, officials said the project was on schedule to begin commercial production around October 1998 and were optimistic about the mine's prospects.
"We're confident we're going to have a very successful mine," said Jim Rothwell, president of BHP's diamonds subsidiary. "We expect this project to be profitable early in its operation."
BHP is in partnership with Canada's Dia Met Minerals Ltd., which has 29 percent of the project, and the two geologists who discovered the diamonds and are part owners of Dia Met.

The Lac de Gras mine is expected to produce about four percent of the world's annual diamond supply in volume terms, yielding revenues of about C$500 million ($365 million) a year for at least 25 years. Much of the output will consist of gems, the most prized and lucrative segment of the market.

At BHP's Koala Camp construction site, eight construction cranes are at work, the steel framework of the ore processing plant rises from the tundra, helicopters buzz overhead, lakes are being drained and bulldozers and tractors strip away surface rock.
A makeshift exploration camp has been replaced by an impressive self-contained facility for 750 workers complete with squash court, satellite communications, bakery and medical center.
A landing strip, capable of receiving giant Hercules heavy transport planes, handles several flights a day bringing in workers and supplies.
The mine plan calls for five kimberlite pipes, the rock formations that host diamonds, to be mined over 17 years.

With exploration work under way, officials are optimistic the mine life will be extended beyond 25 years. The number of kimberlite pipes found on the property rose by five to 82 in the past few months and would likely hit 100 by the end of the year, officials said.

During the mine's first decade, 9,000 tonnes of ore will be processed a day in a high-security facility using water and a centrifuge to separate the precious stones from waste rock. The final picking will be done with X-rays and involve no human contact.

The prize: about one kilogram (2.2 pounds) of diamonds a day -- enough to fill a coffee can. "We will produce a clean rough diamond packaged untouched by human hands," said project manager Dan Johnson.
The diamonds, high-quality stones rivaling those from South Africa's fabled mines, will be roughly sorted on site for insurance purposes and then flown out to be sold, probably in Antwerp, Belgium.
One question on the minds of diamond miners and buyers around the world is how BHP will market that output.

The Australian company, which has extensive experience in selling more prosaic minerals such as coal, has had talks with De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd whose Central Selling Organization controls about three-quarters of the world's rough diamond trade.

But many industry watchers believe BHP plans to sell at least part of its output outside the CSO directly to customers -- a bold move that would undermine De Beers' dominance. "I think they have already made their decision to go independently but they want to keep De Beers guessing until the end," said one analyst.
Rothwell, BHP's head of the diamond project, said a decision would be announced toward the end of the year.

While he stressed no decision had yet been made, his comments reinforced the impression that BHP was attracted to independent sales. Expressing optimism about the diamond market, he noted several factors that would seem to argue in favor of independent marketing and said the company was keeping its options open.
